Repository Collects and Benchmarks World Models for Autonomous Driving and Robotics

A repository collects and benchmarks recent world model papers for autonomous driving and robotics, serving as a supplement to a survey.

  • “Effective world models must integrate several key components, including perception, instruction following, controllability, physical plausibility, and future prediction.”

item.title: New Developments in One-Shot and Vertical Federated Learning Frameworks
item.description:
New Developments in One-Shot and Vertical Federated Learning Frameworks

Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. Recent updates introduce two new frameworks to address existing limitations in multi-round communication and centralized raw-data pooling: \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving, and VAFL, a Vertical Analytic Federated Learning framework.

🔍 Overview

Existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while prior one-shot methods have mainly focused on perception tasks. To resolve these challenges, \method enables collaborative model training for end-to-end autonomous driving. Meanwhile, VAFL provides a Vertical Analytic Federated Learning framework for organizations holding complementary information, allowing them to collaborate without centralized raw-data pooling.

🧩 How it works

Both frameworks implement unique strategies to optimize collaborative learning:

  • \method Architecture: It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models.
  • VAFL Architecture: This framework fits classification and regression heads on fixed local representations through regularized least squares. It features an agent-assisted protected-computation workflow that supports two-party and multi-party collaboration.
  • VAFL Optimization: To reduce fitting overhead, VAFL uses a full-dimensional equivalent solve that applies block factors directly to the target matrix, avoiding the construction of the full inverse. It also offers two width-reduction strategies:
    • Local spectral projection with coefficient lifting, which compresses the prediction space.
    • Full-dimensional local fitting with low-rank cross-party correction, which retains local components outside the collaboration subspace.

⚙️ Key details

Empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of both methods on standard benchmarks:

  • \method performance on Bench2Drive: Closed-loop evaluation shows that in the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85 (4.07 points higher than prior work). In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, marking the best performance among compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.
  • VAFL evaluation: Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrated the accuracy-cost tradeoffs of the width-reduction strategies as well as their compatibility with diverse frozen backbones. The analysis of predictive performance and training time identified useful operating points and the limits of compression.

#FederatedLearning #AutonomousDriving #MachineLearning #PrivacyPreserving

Source: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation Source: VAFL: A Vertical Analytic Federated Learning Mechanism for Efficient Crowdsourced Services via Closed-Form Solutions

item.title: Bench2Drive 0.0.4 updates training data, metrics, and robustness tests
item.description:
Bench2Drive 0.0.4 updates training data, metrics, and robustness tests

Bench2Drive version 0.0.4 has been released, introducing significant updates to the training data, evaluation protocols, and new modalities for autonomous driving research. The release accompanies the acceptance of Bench2Drive at the NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track.

🧩 How it works

The update introduces a new Think2Drive-collected training set consisting of 44 scenarios and 25 routes, totaling 1,100 routes. Unlike the previous Base set, which had an uneven scenario distribution, the new set is strictly uniform over scenarios. Additionally, a new 3D occupancy (3D occ) modality has been added.

A separate validation set of 220 routes is now available for more reliable evaluation. For quicker model development and ablation studies, a tiny validation set called Dev10 has been proposed. These 10 clips were carefully selected from the official 220 routes to be both difficult and representative with low variance, helping to avoid overfitting the full dataset.

⚙️ Key details

The evaluation protocol has been refined with two new metrics: Driving Efficiency and Driving Smoothness. The penalty for minimum speed in calculating the Drive Score has been removed, and the TickRunTime has been extended from 2000 to 4000 to allow for a more lenient driving evaluation.

Specific bugs and errors have been addressed in this release:

  • Camera Projection: The team_code agents for UniAD and VAD were updated to fix a bug where the back camera’s extrinsic parameters were incorrect during evaluation.
  • Ability Calculation: Typos in the ability calculation were corrected, and multi-ability results were updated. This correction does not affect the driving score or success rate.
  • Dataset Consistency: A bug in the B2D_vad_dataset was identified but left in place to maintain consistency with existing results, as no major influence is anticipated.
  • Python Version Conflict: Bench2Drive-VL enables closed-loop QA for VLM4AD. It provides an efficient communication interface between the VLM environment (Python 3.9+) and CARLA, which is only available for Python 3.7 and 3.8. Users encountering Python version errors should consider this protocol discrepancy.
Component Description
Bench2Drive-Robust Analyzes model performance under real deployment issues, including camera-stream failures, ego-state estimation errors, and compute-control latency.
Bench2Drive-Speed Estimates a new functionality for AD systems: speed customization.
Bench2Drive-VL Enables closed-loop QA of VLM4AD and provides a communication bridge between Python 3.9+ and CARLA.

💡 Why it matters

The update addresses methodological concerns in the field by stating that L2 error is not a meaningful indicator and that authors should stop reporting results on nuScenes open-loop planning. The release notes argue that these numbers are not persuasive and can lead to unjustified conclusions that impede field development. By providing a uniform training set, separate validation splits, and new metrics focused on efficiency and smoothness, the update aims to provide a more reliable and realistic evaluation framework for autonomous driving models.

#Bench2Drive #AutonomousDriving #NeurIPS2024 #Benchmark #CARLA

Source: Thinklab-SJTU/Bench2Drive

item.title: NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge Brings Adaptive Reasoning to On‑Board Autonomous Driving
item.description:
NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge Brings Adaptive Reasoning to On‑Board Autonomous Driving

NVIDIA announced an update to its Alpamayo series with Alpamayo 2 Edge, an adaptive reasoning vision‑language‑action (VLA) model designed for real‑time operation on the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor platform.

🔍 Overview

  • Alpamayo 2 Edge runs on a 2 B‑parameter Nemotron‑based reasoning backbone from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge.
  • It is paired with a diffusion action expert to turn surround‑camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs into Chain‑of‑Causation (CoC) reasoning traces and future driving trajectories.
  • The model is built for edge deployment, preserving reasoning quality while fitting the inference budget of an onboard stack.

🧩 How it works

Component Role
Alpamayo 2 Edge Adaptive VLA model that generates reasoning only when needed
Nemotron 2 B backbone (Cosmos 3 Edge) Core reasoning engine
Diffusion action expert Generates driving actions from reasoning traces
AlpaJudge (RB & RF) Human‑calibrated evaluation and reward model for reasoning traces
AlpaGym Closed‑loop reinforcement‑learning environment
  • Adaptive reasoning reduces unnecessary token generation, conserving inference compute during routine driving.
  • Multi‑resolution inputs encode surround‑view observations online.
  • Speculative decoding with DFlash2 accelerates online reasoning without sacrificing quality.
  • Offline distillation uses CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super.
  • Quantization and inference acceleration recipes are provided for NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT‑Edge‑LLM.

⚙️ Key details

  • Post‑trained with closed‑loop RL in NVIDIA AlpaGym, improving closed‑loop driving performance by 48.9 % over the best checkpoint without closed‑loop RL.
  • Uses AlpaJudge to evaluate reasoning traces, select higher‑value training data, and provide RL rewards.
  • The inference script consumes surround‑view camera streams, navigation text, and historical ego‑motion to output CoC reasoning and trajectory predictions.

📈 Performance

  • In early simulation tests, Edge kept its lane in more than twice as many runs as Alpamayo 1.5, recovered from lane offsets ~40 % more often, and planned roughly twice as fast as a hand‑tuned Alpamayo 1.5 server on the same GPU.
  • Zero‑shot evaluation showed a 13.6 % reduction in displacement error (minADE) and a 46.1 % reduction in lateral prediction error (RMSE at 3 s) compared to Alpamayo 2 Super, despite sensor differences.
  • Fine‑tuning on proprietary driving data delivered an additional 44.2 % reduction in displacement error versus the Alpamayo 2 Edge baseline.
  • Within 48 hours, Alpamayo 2 Edge ran at 10 Hz on AGX Thor for real‑time planning.
  • Early access users reported running closed‑loop on NuRec reconstructions of London street recordings within days of receiving the model.

🚀 Availability

  • Early adopters were able to move from model receipt to first real‑vehicle tests within a few days.
  • The repository includes an inference script and recipes for quantization and acceleration, enabling developers to integrate reasoning‑based driving into an onboard stack.

#NVIDIA #AutonomousDriving #EdgeAI #ReinforcementLearning

Source: Running AV Reasoning Models Within Onboard Compute and Latency Limits | NVIDIA Technical Blog
